entries.answer: Serendipity is a fortunate accident, a good outcome that came about by chance rather than by planning, and the detail that makes the word interesting is who it was made for. It was coined in 1754 by Horace Walpole, who wrote it after a happy discovery of a Prince of Wales story he had not been looking for, and he credited it to a Persian phrase meaning the three princes of Serendip, a place name. The word is used in two slightly different ways and the difference is worth knowing: a serendipitous discovery is one where the thing found was better than the thing searched for, while a purely lucky outcome is not serendipity at all, since serendipity specifically involves a person being observant enough to recognise the lucky find. That is the part people miss when they use the word as a synonym for any luck at all.

entries.answer: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time, and its opposite is a word most people know well: permanent. It describes a thing that exists briefly by its nature rather than a thing that merely happens to be brief, so an ephemeral flower, a fading fashion and a very short speech are all properly described, while a long film is not. The word comes from a root meaning for a day or a short span, which is the whole of its history and the whole of its sense. It is worth knowing because it does not simply mean temporary, since a temporary thing might last a year and an ephemeral one lasts a morning, and a person looking for a strong word for brief is looking for this one. It also has an antonym that is easy to confuse with it, since permanent is about duration and eternal is about having no end at all.

entries.answer: Ubiquitous means present everywhere, or so common that noticing it is odd, and the word is used far more than the situation usually deserves. It began as a technical term, meaning present in a fluid at the same concentration everywhere, and it moved into ordinary speech as a strong word for something that is simply very widespread. That is the risk: a thing being common is not the same as a thing being everywhere, so using the word claims more than is usually meant. It is also an excellent word for technology, since the number of things that quietly depend on a network connection or a data centre has grown to the point where the honest answer to many how-does-this-work questions is that it does not work alone. A related family exists for the opposite, from rare, and the same exaggeration applies in the other direction.
